title: Unions, narrowing and exhaustiveness
summary: Discriminated unions that make impossible states unrepresentable, every narrowing check the compiler understands and where narrowing silently stops, exhaustiveness with `never` and `assertNever`, user-defined type guards and assertion functions (trusted, not checked), validating `unknown` input, and the strictness flags that decide how much the checker catches.
prerequisiteNotes: ts-types-basics: union and literal types, the basic narrowing checks, and `unknown` versus `any` versus `never`. This lesson builds on those to model whole state machines, prove a `switch` handles every case, and write guards you can trust.
objectives: Model a request lifecycle as a discriminated union so that states such as 'loading with an error' cannot be constructed.
Narrow with `typeof`, `in`, `instanceof`, equality and a discriminant, and explain the cases where TypeScript keeps or drops a narrowing.
Make a `switch` exhaustive with an `assertNever(x: never): never` helper so that adding a variant becomes a compile error at every unhandled site.
Write user-defined type guards (`x is T`) and assertion functions (`asserts x is T`), and explain why the compiler trusts their bodies without checking them.
Validate untrusted JSON from `unknown` by composing small guards, without `any` or `as`.
Say what `strict` turns on, and what `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds that `strict` does not.

concepts.title: Make impossible states unrepresentable
concepts.body: A 'bag of optionals' such as `{ status: string; data?: T; error?: string }` allows 2 x 2 x infinity combinations, most of them nonsense: loading with data, success with an error, success without data. Every reader must guess which fields go together, and every access needs a `?.` or `!`. A **discriminated union** (tagged union) lists the legal states instead: each member has a literal **discriminant** (`status: 'loading'`) and exactly the fields that state owns. The compiler then rejects an illegal literal at construction, and checking the tag narrows the whole object, so `s.data` is available only after `s.status === 'success'`. The discriminant must be a literal type (string, number, boolean, `null` or `undefined`) shared by every member; a plain `string` tag does not discriminate. Carry per-state data in the state that needs it, like `attempt` on both `loading` and `failure`, rather than at the top level.

concepts.title: Every way to narrow, and where narrowing stops
concepts.body: The checker narrows a union along these runtime checks: `typeof x === 'string'` (primitives and `'function'`; remember `typeof null === 'object'`), `x instanceof C` (classes only, never interfaces, because interfaces are erased), `'key' in x` (keeps the members that declare `key`, even optionally; since TS 4.9 an unlisted key adds `Record<'key', unknown>`), equality with a literal or `null` (`x == null` removes both `null` and `undefined`), and a discriminant check on a property. Aliased conditions such as `const isOk = r.ok; if (isOk)` also narrow when `r` is a `const` or an unreassigned parameter (TS 4.4), and checking one **destructured** `const` field narrows its siblings (TS 4.6). Narrowing is **dropped** inside callbacks for `let` variables that are reassigned after the closure is created, and it is **not** dropped after a function call, even one that mutates the object: property narrowings are optimistic. Since TS 5.5, `xs.filter(x => x !== null)` infers a type predicate, but `filter(Boolean)` still does not.

concepts.title: Exhaustiveness with never and assertNever
concepts.body: Each `case` removes one member from the union, so after the last one the remaining type is `never`. Passing it to `function assertNever(x: never): never` therefore compiles, and the day someone adds a `'hexagon'` variant the leftover type becomes the hexagon member, which is not assignable to `never`: every `switch` that forgot it turns into a compile error pointing at the default. That is the real payoff of discriminated unions in a large codebase. At runtime the helper throws, which also catches data from an older or newer server that does not match the types. Alternatives: `const _exhaustive: never = s;` or `throw new Error(String(s satisfies never))`. An annotated return type gives a weaker signal (TS2366, 'lacks ending return statement'), and only when the function returns a value, so prefer the explicit helper. `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` (on in this runtime) additionally rejects a non-empty case that falls into the next one.

concepts.title: Type guards and assertion functions are trusted, not checked
concepts.body: A function returning `value is T` is a **user-defined type guard**: when it returns `true` the caller's argument narrows to `T`, and when it returns `false` it narrows to the rest. An **assertion function** returning `asserts value is T` (or `asserts cond`) narrows everything after the call and must throw otherwise; it needs an explicit type annotation on the call target, so `const assertX = (v: unknown): asserts v is X => ...` fails at the call site with TS2775 unless the variable itself is annotated. The catch: the compiler only checks that the body returns a `boolean` (or nothing). It never checks that the body proves the claim, so `return 'name' in x` typed as `x is User` makes `{ name: 42 }` a `User`, and an empty assertion body asserts everything. Treat guards like tiny parsers: check every field you rely on, keep them next to the type, and test them with bad input. Prefer a guard over `as`, because the lie is at least confined to one tested function.

concepts.title: unknown at the boundary: compose small guards
concepts.body: `JSON.parse`, `catch (e)`, message events and storage reads hand you values of unknown shape. Typing them `any` silences the checker everywhere the value flows; typing them `unknown` forces a check before use. Validation scales by **composition**: a reusable `isRecord(v): v is Record<string, unknown>` (object, not null, not an array), a few leaf guards (`isFiniteNumber`, `isNonEmptyString`), then one guard or assertion per domain type that switches on the discriminant and checks that variant's fields. Destructure fields into locals before narrowing them, which narrows reliably and reads well. Return a result union (`{ ok: true; value } | { ok: false; error }`) or throw a `TypeError` with a path such as `lines[2]: invalid item` so the caller knows what failed. Under `strict`, `catch (e)` is `unknown` too (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`), so narrow with `e instanceof Error` before reading `e.message`.

concepts.title: Strictness flags decide what narrowing can catch
concepts.body: `strict: true` (what this runtime uses) switches on a family of flags, including `strictNullChecks` (`null` and `undefined` are separate types, so `string | null` must be narrowed before use; without it, every type silently includes them and none of this lesson works), `noImplicitAny` (an unannotated parameter that cannot be inferred is an error instead of a silent `any`), `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `strictFunctionTypes` and `strictPropertyInitialization`. Two useful flags are **not** in `strict`. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes `arr[i]` and `record[key]` include `| undefined`, so an empty array or a missing key must be handled; this runtime does not enable it, so `[][0].toFixed()` type-checks here and throws. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes a missing property from one explicitly set to `undefined`. Mention both when asked how you would harden a codebase; turning on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in an existing project usually surfaces real bugs along with some noise in loops that already check bounds.

task: Write `transition(state, event)`, the reducer for a request lifecycle. Declare `type RequestState` as a discriminated union on `status`: `idle`; `loading` with `attempt: number`; `success` with `data: string[]`; `failure` with `error: string` and `attempt: number`. Declare `type RequestEvent` as a union on `type`: `FETCH`, `RESOLVE` (with `data`), `REJECT` (with `error`), `RETRY` and `RESET`. Rules: `FETCH` starts `loading` with attempt 1 from any state except `loading`, which is returned unchanged; `RESOLVE` turns `loading` into `success` and `REJECT` turns it into `failure` with the same attempt, while in any other state they are stale and the state is returned unchanged; `RETRY` turns a `failure` with attempt below 3 into `loading` with attempt + 1, otherwise nothing changes; `RESET` always returns `idle`. Switch on the event and end with `default: return assertNever(event)` using a helper `assertNever(value: never): never`, so a new event type cannot be forgotten.
hints: Write the two unions first. `state.status === 'loading'` then makes `state.attempt` available, and `case 'RESOLVE':` makes `event.data` available, so no `?.` or `!` is needed anywhere.

Inside `switch (event.type)` each case is a single expression: check the current `state.status`, build the next state literal, or return `state` itself when the event is stale. The `default` branch sees `event: never` and returns `assertNever(event)`.
checklist: Both `RequestState` and `RequestEvent` are discriminated unions with literal tags; no field is optional.
No `?.`, `!`, `as` or `any`: each field is read only after narrowing.
Stale `RESOLVE`/`REJECT` events and a `RETRY` at the attempt limit return the unchanged state.
The switch ends in `default: return assertNever(event)`, so adding a variant is a compile error.
pitfalls: Modelling state as one object with optional `data?`, `error?` and `loading: boolean` flags, which allows contradictory combinations and forces `!` everywhere.
Using `string` instead of a literal type for the tag: `{ kind: string }` does not discriminate, so checking it narrows nothing.
Ending a switch with `default: return 0` or no default at all, which silently swallows a newly added variant instead of making it a compile error.
Writing a type guard that checks one field (`'name' in x`) and claims the whole type; the compiler trusts the predicate and the crash happens far away.
Leaving an assertion function body empty or under-checking it, which narrows everything after the call with no runtime proof.
Expecting narrowing to be reset after a function call that mutates the object; property narrowings are optimistic and stay in place.
Using `instanceof` on an interface or on a plain object that merely has the class's shape; it checks the prototype chain, not the structure.
Assuming `arr[0]` is safe because it type-checks: without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` an empty array gives `undefined` typed as the element type.

walkthrough.title: Read the reducer as a state machine
walkthrough.body: Before writing code, draw the states as boxes and the events as arrows: that picture is the spec. `FETCH` leaves `idle` (and `success` or `failure`) for `loading`; `loading` resolves to `success` or rejects to `failure`; a `failure` can `RETRY` back to `loading` while attempts remain; `RESET` returns to `idle` from anywhere. Any arrow not drawn is a no-op, which is how stale responses are ignored. Interviewers like to ask what happens when a `RESOLVE` arrives after a `RESET`; with this model the answer is 'nothing', because only `loading` accepts it. Saying that out loud shows you designed for races, not just the happy path.

walkthrough.title: Adding a variant: let the compiler find every switch
walkthrough.body: Suppose product asks for a `CANCEL` event. Add `| { type: 'CANCEL' }` to `RequestEvent` and compile. Every `switch (event.type)` that ends with `assertNever(event)` now fails with 'Argument of type `{ type: 'CANCEL' }` is not assignable to parameter of type `never`', so the compiler gives you a to-do list of every reducer, logger and serializer that must decide what cancelling means. Without the helper, those switches would fall through to a default that returns the old state and the feature would ship half done. The same works for state: a new `status: 'stale'` lights up every `render` and every `transition` branch that inspects it.

walkthrough.title: Solve the task in three moves
walkthrough.body: First, write the types and say why: 'four states, each owning its fields; five events, each carrying its payload; impossible combinations do not type-check'. Second, write `switch (event.type)` with one case per event; inside each, narrow `state.status` with a ternary and either build the next literal or return `state` unchanged. Third, add `default: return assertNever(event)` and mention the runtime benefit: a malformed event from a WebSocket throws loudly. Close with cost (O(1), at most one allocation) and the follow-up you would offer: lift the attempt limit into a parameter, or add a `CANCEL` event and let the compiler show every place that must handle it.

extraPractice.title: A shape guard you can trust
extraPractice.prompt: Write `isShape(value: unknown): value is Shape` for `type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'rect'; width: number; height: number }`. Return `true` only for a plain object (not `null`, not an array) whose `kind` is `'circle'` with a finite, non-negative number `radius`, or `'rect'` with finite, non-negative numbers `width` and `height`. Extra properties are allowed. Anything else, including other kinds, strings and arrays, returns `false` without throwing.
hints: Start with `isRecord(v): v is Record<string, unknown>` so you can read `value.kind` safely, then switch on it.
A small `isSize(v: unknown): v is number` guard that checks `typeof`, `Number.isFinite` and `>= 0` keeps each case one line.
checklist: `null`, arrays, strings and `{}` return `false` instead of throwing.
Every field the type promises is checked, including its sign.
The return type is `value is Shape`, so callers get `kind` and the variant's fields after the check.

extraPractice.title: Checkout with an assertion function
extraPractice.prompt: Declare `type Line` as a union of `{ kind: 'item'; sku: string; price: number; qty: number }`, `{ kind: 'discount'; percent: number }` and `{ kind: 'shipping'; cost: number }`, plus `interface Order { lines: Line[] }` and `type CheckoutResult = { ok: true; total: number } | { ok: false; error: string }`. Write `assertOrder(value: unknown): asserts value is Order` that throws a `TypeError` for the first problem: `'expected { lines: [...] }'` if there is no `lines` array; then for line `i`, `'lines[i]: expected an object'`, `'lines[i]: invalid item'` (non-empty `sku`, finite `price` >= 0, integer `qty` >= 1), `'lines[i]: invalid discount'` (`percent` from 0 to 100), `'lines[i]: invalid shipping'` (finite `cost` >= 0) or `'lines[i]: unknown kind'`. Then write `checkout(input: unknown): CheckoutResult`: catch the assertion error into `{ ok: false, error }`; otherwise total = items subtotal x (1 - min(sum of percents, 100) / 100) + shipping, rounded to cents with `Math.round(total * 100) / 100`. Handle the lines with an exhaustive switch.
hints: Write `assertLine(value: unknown, at: string): asserts value is Line` and call it for each element from `assertOrder`; destructure each variant's fields into locals before checking them.
After `assertOrder(input)` returns, `input` is an `Order`, so `for (const line of input.lines)` with `switch (line.kind)` and `default: assertNever(line)` needs no casts.
checklist: The assertion function checks every field of every variant before the compiler starts trusting `Order`.
The first invalid line wins and the error message names its index.
Discounts are capped at 100 percent, shipping is never discounted, and an empty order totals 0.

followUps.question: Why not model the request as `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: string }`?
followUps.answer: It admits states the program never means: loading with an error, success without data, data and error together. Every consumer has to defend against them with `?.` and `!`, and nothing stops a reducer from producing them. A discriminated union lists the four legal states, the compiler rejects the rest at construction, and checking the tag gives you exactly the fields that exist.

followUps.question: What does `assertNever` buy you over `default: return state`?
followUps.answer: At compile time, `assertNever(x: never)` only type-checks while every variant is handled, so adding one turns every unhandled switch into an error that names the missing member. At runtime it throws on data that does not match the types (an old client, a new server), instead of silently doing nothing. A plain default hides both problems.

followUps.question: Your guard `isUser(x): x is User` returns `'name' in x`. What can go wrong and how would you fix it?
followUps.answer: The compiler never checks that the body proves the predicate, so `{ name: 42 }` passes and is typed as `User`; the crash happens later at `user.name.toUpperCase()`. Check every field you depend on with its type, test the guard with malformed inputs, or generate the guard from a schema library (Zod, Valibot) so the type and the check come from one definition.

followUps.question: Which compiler flags would you turn on for a new TypeScript service and why?
followUps.answer: `strict` for `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` and the rest; then `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` so array and record lookups include `undefined`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` so missing and `undefined` differ, and `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`. They cost a few extra checks but catch empty-array crashes and half-handled switches at compile time.

followUps.question: When does TypeScript keep a narrowing that is no longer true at runtime?
followUps.answer: Property narrowings survive function calls: after `if (box.state.status === 'loading') { reset(); box.state.attempt }` the checker still believes `loading`, even if `reset` replaced the state. It is a deliberate trade-off for usability. Copy the value into a `const` before calling out, or re-check after the call. Guards and assertion functions with weak bodies are the other source of narrowings that lie.

takeaways: Model states as a discriminated union with a literal tag; impossible combinations then fail to compile.
Narrow with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality or the tag; property narrowings are optimistic and survive function calls.
End every switch over a union with `assertNever(x: never)`, so a new variant is a compile error and bad data throws.
Type guards and assertion functions are trusted, not checked: test them like parsers.
Validate `unknown` with small composed guards; `strict` does not include `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.

diagrams.title: The request lifecycle as a tagged union
diagrams.alt: State machine with four states. RESET leads from any state to idle. FETCH moves idle to loading, which carries an attempt number. RESOLVE moves loading to success, which carries data. REJECT moves loading to failure, which carries an error and the attempt. RETRY from failure goes to a decision, attempt below 3, which leads back to loading with attempt plus one.
diagrams.caption: Each box is one union member with only its own fields; an event with no arrow from the current state is a no-op.

steps.text: `FETCH` from `idle` builds `{ status: 'loading', attempt: 1 }`. It does the same from `success` or `failure`; in `loading` it is ignored.
`RESOLVE` is accepted only in `loading`. The new `success` object carries `data`; a stale `RESOLVE` in any other state returns the state unchanged.
`REJECT` also needs `loading`, and copies `state.attempt` into the `failure`, which is only readable after narrowing on `status`.
`RETRY` in `failure` goes back to `loading` with `attempt + 1` while attempts remain; at 3 the failure stays.
`RESET` returns `{ status: 'idle' }` from any state, dropping every field the old state had.

diagrams.title: How a switch narrows a union down to never
diagrams.alt: Narrowing flow for s of type Shape, a union of circle, rect and tri. Each case check peels one member off to the right: circle, rect and triangle. What falls through every check reaches default with type never, where assertNever(s) compiles. A new hex kind without a case would reach the default with type Hex, which is a compile error.
diagrams.caption: Each case removes a member; only when none is left does the default see never, so a forgotten variant cannot compile.

steps.text: Comparing the discriminant with `'circle'` narrows the true branch to the circle member, so `s.r` is readable.
On the false branch the circle is gone: `s` is `Rect | Tri`, and the next case peels off `Rect`.
Only `Tri` is left before the last case.
Nothing is left for the default: `s` is `never`, so `assertNever(s)` type-checks.
Add `{ kind: 'hex' }` to the union without a case and the default sees `Hex`, which is not assignable to `never`: compile error at every forgotten switch.

diagrams.title: Bag of optionals versus a tagged union
diagrams.alt: Comparison of two ways to type a request. On the left, status is a string with optional data and error: a loading state with data compiles, and a success state may lack data so every read needs a non-null assertion. On the right, status is a literal tag with four exact shapes: loading with data is a compile error, and narrowing to success guarantees data is a string array.
diagrams.caption: Optional fields describe every combination; a tagged union describes only the legal ones.

diagrams.title: A type guard that lies
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with your code, the type checker and the runtime. The checker sees isUser returning x is User and narrows data to User without examining the body. At runtime the guard only checks that a name key exists, so the object with name 42 passes. Calling data.name.toUpperCase() then throws a TypeError far from the guard.
diagrams.caption: The compiler trusts a predicate's signature, not its body; a weak guard moves the crash somewhere else.

messages.label: data: User
messages.note: Only the return type is used; the body is never compared with the claim.

messages.label: TypeError
messages.note: The crash is reported here, not in the guard that lied.

diagrams.title: Indexing an array with and without noUncheckedIndexedAccess
diagrams.alt: Comparison of reading scores[0] from an empty number array. With strict only, the read is typed number, so calling toFixed compiles and throws a TypeError at runtime. With noUncheckedIndexedAccess the read is typed number or undefined, so the code must check or default the value before calling toFixed.
diagrams.caption: `strict` does not cover indexing; `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes every lookup admit it may be missing.

predict.explain: The compiler trusts the predicate signature and narrows `v` to `number`, so `v + 1` type-checks. At runtime the guard returned `true` for a string, and `'42' + 1` concatenates to `'421'`.

`strict` does not include `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, so `scores[0]` is typed `number` even though it is `undefined` at runtime, and calling a method on `undefined` throws. With the flag, `top` would be `number | undefined` and the call would not compile.

Typing is structural, so a plain object with the right fields is assignable to `HttpError`. `instanceof` checks the prototype chain at runtime, and this object was never constructed by the class. A `#private` field or a discriminant property makes such fakes impossible to type.

The `as Shape[]` cast is unchecked, so the `hex` object reaches `area`. No case matches, the default runs, and `assertNever` throws with the offending value. Without the default the function would return `undefined` despite its `number` return type.

Property narrowings are not invalidated by function calls, so the checker still believes `box.state` is the loading member. `reset` replaced it with `{ status: 'idle' }`, which has no `attempt`, so the read is `undefined`. Copy the value into a `const` before calling out, or re-check afterwards.

`filter(Boolean)` drops every falsy value, including the `0` you wanted to keep, and its type is not narrowed. The arrow `c => c !== null` keeps `0`, and TypeScript 5.5 infers it as a type predicate, so `present` is `number[]`.

lab.tip: Draw the states as boxes before typing: one box per union member with its own fields, one arrow per event. Then say the two sentences interviewers listen for: 'impossible states do not type-check' and 'the default calls `assertNever`, so a new variant is a compile error and bad data throws'. If the input comes from outside, add a third: 'it arrives as `unknown`, and my guard checks every field because the compiler trusts it blindly'.
